column2: From Arabic Sayḥān: the name of Seyhun (the Syr Darya), one of the rivers of paradise, transferred to the Saros River in Cilicia
column3: The Saros, which descends from the Taurus and flows through the heart of Adana, came to be called after the Central Asian Seyhun following the Arab conquests; Islamic geographers interpreted the Seyhan and the Ceyhan as rivers of paradise. Adana's Roman-era Stone Bridge (Taşköprü) spans this river, and the Seyhan Dam was completed in 1956. One of Adana's central districts also bears the river's name.

column2: From the name of the Kozanoğulları, the feudal family that ruled the region; the earlier name was Sis, capital of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
column3: Sis, capital of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia from 1186 to 1375, holds an important place in Armenian church history as the seat of the Catholicosate. The name of the Kozanoğulları, who dominated the region in the 18th and 19th centuries, was given to the sanjak after the Fırka-i Islahiye (Reform Division) campaign of 1865, and to the town itself in 1923. The word Kozan is associated with Turkish koz "walnut".

column2: From the Greek city name Anazarbos; the Arabic ʿAyn Zarba "spring of Zarba" is a folk interpretation
column3: Anazarbos, set against a rocky hill in the eastern Çukurova, was the capital of the Roman province of Cilicia Secunda; the physician Dioscorides was born here. The Arabs reinterpreted the name as ʿAyn Zarba, using the word for "spring"; the fortress of the Armenian kings of Cilicia stands on the hilltop. The Turkish form Anavarza derives from the Arabic pronunciation.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of Greek akrōtḗri "cape, peninsula"; the town stands on a peninsula jutting into the lake
column3: The town, built on a peninsula reaching into Turkey's second-largest freshwater lake, was known in the Byzantine period by the Greek word akrotiri "cape"; the name, which took the form Eğridir in Turkish, was also linked to the Turkish word eğri "crooked". The town was the seat of the Hamitoğulları, and the Dündar Bey Madrasa and Hızır Bey Mosque still stand there. In the 1980s the name was corrected to Eğirdir.

column2: Old Turkic yalavaç "envoy, prophet": the name the Turks gave to Pisidian Antioch, where Saint Paul preached
column3: Pisidian Antioch, founded by the Seleucids, is the city where Saint Paul preached on his first missionary journey; it grew as a Roman colony under Augustus. The Turks, either because they knew it as the city of the Christian apostle or in memory of a local saint, named the town with the Old Turkic word yalavaç, "envoy, prophet"; the word appears in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. The Devlethan Mosque is a Seljuk work.

column2: A city name from the Pisidian language; the Ottoman village of Ağlasun is the Turkish pronunciation of this name
column3: Sagalassos, perched 1,500 meters up in the Taurus Mountains, was the most magnificent of the Pisidian cities that Alexander the Great took by force in 333 BC; its Antonine Nymphaeum and theater have been re-erected. The village's name, Ağlasun, is the Turkish folk pronunciation of the ancient name and a fine example of how ancient names survive in village names.

column2: From the place name Ablasta in Hittite texts; the town on the source plain of the Ceyhan
column3: The town on the source plain of the Ceyhan River appears in Hittite documents as Ablasta; Byzantine and Arab sources carried the same name forward. The Battle of Elbistan, in which the Mamluk sultan Baybars defeated the Mongols in 1277, was fought here, and the town was the first seat of the Dulkadirid principality. The Late Hittite inscriptions at Karahöyük bear witness to the antiquity of the name.

column2: Old Persian Katpatuka "land of beautiful horses" (the common interpretation); also linked to Hittite katta peda "lower land"
column3: The satrapy listed as Katpatuka in the Behistun inscription of the Persian king Darius was known to Greek writers as Kappadokia; the name is interpreted as Old Persian "land of beautiful horses", though a derivation from Hittite katta peda "lower land" has also been proposed. Herodotus refers to the Cappadocians as Syrians. The fairy chimneys, rock churches and underground cities are carved into the region's volcanic tuff.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era settlement name Korama; folk etymology explains it through Turkish görme "unseen" (a hidden, invisible place)
column3: Cappadocia's valley of rock churches appears in Byzantine hagiographies under the name Korama; the name, which became Göreme in Turkish, is popularly interpreted as the "unseen" village of Christians hiding from Arab raids. Known as Maçan in the Ottoman period, the village regained the name Göreme in the 1980s; its Open-Air Museum is on the UNESCO list.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Greek phrase Hagios Prokopios "Saint Procopius"
column3: Cappadocia's rock-carved town was known in the Byzantine period as Hagios Prokopios after its church dedicated to Saint Procopius; the local Greeks called it Prokopi until 1923. The name took the form Ürküp and then Ürgüp in Turkish, and appears thus in Ottoman documents. Winemaking and fairy chimneys are the town's emblems.

column2: From the name of the sanctuary of Venasa (Ouenasa), famed for its temple of Zeus and mentioned by Strabo
column3: The potters' town on the banks of the Kızılırmak stands on the site Strabo described as the Cappadocian sanctuary of Zeus Venasa, with its three thousand temple slaves. The Greek name Ouenasa became Avanos in Turkish. Red-clay pottery, practiced continuously since Hittite times, is the town's identity.

column2: From the Hattic city name Hattuš; capital of the Hittite Empire, where the Hittite language "nešili" was deciphered
column3: The Hattian city of Ḫattuš became the capital of the Hittite king Hattušili I in the 17th century BC; the king took his name from the city. The tablet copy of the Treaty of Kadesh and thirty thousand cuneiform tablets were found here; the Lion Gate and the Yerkapı tunnel are parts of the fortifications. The Ottoman village of Boğazköy was renamed Boğazkale in the 1950s; the site is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

column2: Turkish alaca "mottled, multicolored" + höyük "mound": from the mound's colored soil layers
column3: The mound, famous for its pre-Hittite Bronze Age royal tombs, is named with the Turkish words alaca and höyük; whether its Hittite name was Arinna (city of the Sun Goddess) is debated. The excavation begun in 1935 at Atatürk's request was the first major project of Turkish archaeology; the sun disks were found here. The word höyük comes from the Old Turkic form üyük.

column2: From the name of the Phrygian king Gordias; capital of Midas and the city where the "Gordian knot" was cut
column3: The Phrygian capital on the banks of the Sakarya bears the name of Gordias, who according to legend arrived in the city on an ox-cart and became king; the tumulus of King Midas preserves one of the world's oldest wooden structures. Alexander the Great cut the famous knot with his sword here in 333 BC. Excavations beside the Ottoman village of Yassıhöyük have continued since 1950.

column2: Persian pūlād "steel" (Turkish polat) + -lı: the village of a person named Polat, or of a place hard as steel
column3: The steppe town west of Ankara is named with the word polat, derived from Persian pūlād "steel" and also used in Turkish as a personal name. The town was the center of the Battle of Sakarya in 1921 and neighbors the Phrygian capital of Gordion. Polat is widespread in Mongolian and the Turkic languages with the meaning "steel".

column2: Turkish bey + Persian pazar "market": from the market founded by a Germiyan bey; the ancient name was Lagania
column3: The town on the site of the Roman road station Lagania was known in the Turkish period as Beğpazarı, a weekly market founded by a bey. Ottoman mansions, silverwork and carrot farming define the town; the Suluhan caravanserai is a trace of the Silk Road. The word bey comes from the Old Turkic form beg.

column2: Mongolian ulus "people, nation": a word revived during the Language Reform (1930s) as the equivalent of millet; the square of the First Grand National Assembly
column3: Ankara's old center, Taşhan Square, was the heart of the War of Independence with its First Assembly building and Victory Monument. In the 1930s the square was named with the word ulus, which had passed from Mongolian into Old Turkic and was revived in the Language Reform as the equivalent of millet "nation". The Temple of Augustus and the Hacı Bayram Mosque stand in the same quarter.

column2: Turkish çan "bell" + kaya "rock": from rocks that ring like a bell, or from a rock facing Çankırı; the quarter of the Presidential Mansion
column3: The vineyard house on the hill south of Ankara, presented to Mustafa Kemal in 1921, became the Presidential Mansion; the quarter's name comes from the old name of the vineyard area and is linked to the words çan and kaya. Çankaya, home to the embassies and the Grand National Assembly, is the political center of the Republic's capital.

column2: Turkish kızıl "red" + ay "moon": from the name Kızılay adopted by the Hilâl-i Ahmer Society in 1935; the square in front of the society's headquarters
column3: The Ottoman Hilâl-i Ahmer (Red Crescent) Society, founded in 1868, adopted the Turkish equivalent Kızılay as its name in 1935; the square in front of its headquarters in Yenişehir came to be known by this name. The word kızıl appears in the Orkhon Inscriptions in the Old Turkic form kızıl "red". Güvenpark and Atatürk Boulevard form the axis of the quarter.

column2: Turkish ak "white" + Persian şehir "city": "white city"; the town where Nasreddin Hoca lived, ancient Philomelion
column3: Philomelion, at the foot of the Sultan Mountains, was a Byzantine fortress on the road to Konya; the Seljuks called it Akşehir for its white-stone houses and snow-capped mountains. It is known for the tomb of Nasreddin Hoca and as the place where Yıldırım Bayezid died as Timur's captive after the Battle of Ankara in 1402. Cherry growing and the Nasreddin Hoca festivals are synonymous with the town.

column2: Turkish bey + Persian şehir "city": the "bey's city" built up by Süleyman Bey, founder of the Eşrefoğlu principality
column3: The town on the shore of Lake Beyşehir is the principality seat founded by Eşrefoğlu Süleyman Bey at the end of the 13th century on the site of Viranşehir; its name means "the bey's city". The wooden-columned Eşrefoğlu Mosque (1299) is the largest wooden mosque in Anatolia. The Hittite rock monument of Eflatunpınar and the Kubadabad Palace on the lakeshore are traces of two separate ages.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of Greek Herakleia "city of Herakles"; one of three places in Anatolia bearing the name Ereğli
column3: Kybistra, at the northern mouth of the Taurus passes, bore the name Herakleia, dedicated to Herakles, in the Roman period; it appears as Hiraqla in the Arab raids, and Harun al-Rashid took the city in 806. The name, Ereğli in Turkish, derives from the same Greek name in Karadeniz Ereğli and Marmara Ereğlisi. The Late Hittite rock relief at İvriz lies within the district.

column2: Turkish çatal "fork" + höyük "mound": a "forked" mound formed of two adjacent hills
column3: The Neolithic settlement on the Konya Plain, dating back to 7400 BC, is one of the world's oldest towns; wall paintings and mother-goddess figurines were found in this settlement, whose houses were entered through the roofs. Its Turkish name comes from the forked appearance of the mound, which consists of an eastern and a western hill. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

column2: Turkish kül "ash" + tepe "hill": from the mound's ash-colored soil; the ancient name was Kaneš/Neša, the source of the Hittites' name for their language, "nešili"
column3: The karum of Kaniš, founded by Assyrian merchants in the 20th century BC, yielded the oldest written documents in Anatolia, some 23,000 cuneiform tablets. The Hittites called this city Neša and named their own language "nešili" after it. The Turkish name Kültepe comes from the ash-colored soil of the mound, dug for centuries as fertilizer. Excavations have continued since 1948.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Greek mountain name Argaios, from argós "bright, white"; the volcanic peak of Cappadocia
column3: Argaios, which Strabo described as a peak "from which both seas can be seen", is an extinct volcano of 3,917 meters depicted on the ancient coins of Kayseri; its name is explained by the Greek word for "bright, white". The mountain, Erciyes in Turkish, is the volcano that erupted the tuff of Cappadocia. A ski resort and Yörük summer pastures lie on its slopes.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era fortress name Tephrike; the 9th-century capital of the Paulicians
column3: Tephrike, capital of the Paulician sect in the 9th century, appears in Byzantine and Arab sources; in Turkish it took the form Divriği. The Great Mosque and Hospital built in 1228 by the Mengücek ruler Ahmed Şah are on the UNESCO list as the pinnacle of stone carving. The iron mine has been worked for centuries.

column2: From the name of the city Tuwanuwa in Hittite texts; the center of the Late Hittite kingdom of Tabal
column3: The city, Tuwanuwa in Hittite documents and, as Tuwana, the center of the kingdom of Tabal in the Late Hittite period, became famous in Roman times as the birthplace of the philosopher Apollonius. Its Roman aqueducts gave the Ottoman village the name Kemerhisar ("arch fortress"). The İvriz relief of King Warpalawas is a work of this kingdom.

column2: From the name of Hacı Bektaş Veli, founder of the Bektashi order; Arabic ḥācc "pilgrim" + the Persian personal name Bektaş
column3: The lodge of Hacı Bektaş Veli, who came from Khorasan in the 13th century and settled in the village of Sulucakarahöyük, became the spiritual center of the Bektashi order and of the janissary corps; the village came to bear his name. After the closure of the dervish lodges in 1925, the complex became a museum in 1964; commemorative ceremonies are held every August. Bektaş is a personal name of Persian origin.

column2: Turkish sivri "pointed" + Arabic hisar "fortress": from the fortress on pointed crags; the Byzantine name was Iustinianopolis
column3: The town neighboring the Phrygian sacred city of Pessinus bore the name Iustinianopolis in the Byzantine period; the Turks called it Sivrihisar for its fortress on the pointed crags. The wooden-pillared Great Mosque (1274) and the village of Hortu, held to be the birthplace of Nasreddin Hoca, form the town's memory. It was from Pessinus that the black stone of Cybele was carried to Rome.

column2: From the name of Seyyid Battal Gazi, epic hero of the Arab-Byzantine wars; Arabic sayyid "lord, master" + ğāzī "warrior for the faith"
column3: On the hill beside the Byzantine city of Nakoleia, the tomb of Battal Gazi, legendary hero of the 8th-century Arab-Byzantine wars, was built in the 13th century by the mother of a Seljuk sultan; the complex around it became a Bektashi lodge. The epic Battalnâme was read across Anatolia for centuries, and the town bears his name. It lies near the Midas Monument in the Phrygian valley.

column2: Turkish tuz "salt" + göl "lake": Turkey's second-largest lake, named for the salt crust that forms when it dries in summer; the ancient name was Tatta
column3: The shallow lake that Strabo called Tatta and described as a place where "birds' feathers become coated with salt" has supplied Anatolia's salt for centuries. The Turkish word tuz appears in the Orkhon Inscriptions in the Old Turkic form tuz. The lake dries in summer into a white plain and is also known for its flamingo colonies.

column2: Turkish kızıl "red" + ırmak "river": from the red alluvium it carries; Greek Halys "salty", Hittite Marassantiya
column3: Turkey's longest river appears in Hittite texts as Marassantiya and in Greek sources as Halys, because it flowed through salty lands; the prophecy to the Lydian king Croesus, "if you cross the Halys you will destroy a great empire", concerns this river. The Turks called it Kızılırmak for the red alluvium it carries. The word ırmak comes from the Old Turkic form ırmak "river".

column2: Arabic zaʿfarān "saffron" + Greek pólis "city" (Turkish bolu): the city where saffron is grown
column3: The Byzantine fortress of Dadybra appears as Zalifre in Seljuk documents and as Taraklıborlu in Ottoman ones; after the 17th century the name Safranbolu took hold because of the saffron cultivated in the area. The element bolu comes from Greek pólis, and safran from Arabic. The town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its Ottoman timber mansions, is famous for the Cinci Han and the Köprülü Mosque.

column2: The name of the city founded by the Persian princess Amastris (niece of Darius); the earlier name was Sesamos
column3: Sesamos, mentioned by Homer, was refounded around 300 BC by the Persian princess Amastris, wife of the tyrant of Heraclea Pontica, and took her name. The Genoese repaired the fortress in the 13th to 15th centuries; when Mehmed the Conqueror took the city in 1460 he is said to have called it "çeşm-i cihan" (the eye of the world). The town, Amasra in Turkish, is famous for its fortress and harbor.

column2: Persian çahār-şanba "fourth day": from the market held on Wednesday
column3: The town on the Yeşilırmak delta took its name from the large market held on Wednesdays; other Anatolian towns such as Cumapazarı and Perşembe are likewise named after days of the week. The word çarşamba comes from the Persian elements çahār "four" and şanba "day". The Hittite-period settlement of İkiztepe lies nearby on the plain.

column2: From the name of the ancient harbor of Phadisane; in the Roman period Polemonion, after King Polemon
column3: The Black Sea harbor appears as Phadisane in Arrian's Periplus; King Polemon of Pontus refounded the city and named it Polemonion. The Cıngırt Rock near the town, Fatsa in Turkish, is the ancient acropolis. Hazelnuts and fishing are the town's livelihood.

column2: From Greek oínos "wine": Oinoe, "place of vineyards, wine country"
column3: Oinoe on the coast, where Xenophon's army stopped, takes its name from the Greek word for wine; it was a fortress town under Byzantium and the Empire of Trebizond. The town, Ünye in Turkish, prospered in the 18th century as the palace town of Canikli Ali Paşa. Ünye Castle and Çakırtepe are its emblems.

column2: Greek trí- "three" + pólis "city": a city formed of three fortresses or three settlements
column3: Tripolis at the mouth of the Harşit River bore the name "three cities" because of its three fortresses (Saint John, Andoz and Bedrama); the Turkish pronunciation Tirebolu preserves the element -polis as bolu. The town, which joined the Ottoman realm in 1461, lay on the front line in the Ottoman-Russian wars. Hazelnuts and fishing are the basis of its economy.

column2: Arabic şebb "alum" (Turkish şebin) + Karahisar "black fortress": the black fortress famous for its alum mine
column3: The fortress on the site of the Roman military colony of Koloneia was known in the Turkish period as Karahisar; in the 15th to 17th centuries the element Şebin (alum) was added because of the alum mine whose output was sold to Europe. This addition distinguishes it from the other Karahisars of Anatolia. The fortress of King Mithridates of Pontus and the Meryemana Monastery are the town's historic monuments.

column2: Turkish akça "whitish" + Persian ābād "prosperous place"; Greek Platana "plane tree" (Ottoman Pulathane)
column3: The harbor town west of Trabzon bore the Greek name Platana after the plane trees on its shore and was written Pulathane in Ottoman documents. In the 1920s it was given the name Akçaabat, formed from Turkish akça and the Persian-derived element -abat; the same -abat appears in many names from Arnavutköy to Hereke. Akçaabat meatballs and the horon dance are associated with the town.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era valley name Matzouka; the valley of the Sumela Monastery
column3: The mountainous valley south of Trabzon appears as Matzouka in the records of the Empire of Trebizond; the Sumela (Panagia Soumela) Monastery, founded in the 4th century, is built into the cliffs of this valley. The town, Maçka in Turkish, lay on the Iranian transit route with its summer pastures and the Zigana Pass.

column2: Greek óphis "snake": from the name of the winding Of (Solaklı) River
column3: The district with the shortest name in Turkey lies at the mouth of the river that appears as Ophis "snake" in Arrian's Periplus; the name is attributed to the river's winding course. The town, famed for its madrasas in the Ottoman period, gave rise to the saying "the hocas of Of". Tea gardens and the Sultan Murad plateau are its emblems.

column2: From the name of the settlement Sourmena near the harbor of Hyssos mentioned by Xenophon
column3: Sourmena, neighboring the harbor of Hyssos where the Ten Thousand camped before reaching Trabzon, appears in Byzantine records; in Turkish it became Sürmene. The town is known for its ruby-handled knives and wooden boatbuilding, and the Memiş Ağa Mansion is an example of Ottoman civil architecture.

column2: Turkish pazar "market" (of Persian origin): from the weekly market; the ancient name was Athenai (Atina), changed in 1928
column3: The coastal town inhabited by Laz people stands on the site of the ancient harbor that appears in Arrian as Athenai; the name, written Atina in Ottoman times, was changed in 1928 to Pazar, after the town's market, to avoid confusion with the capital of Greece. The Laz language and tea culture are the town's identity; Kız Kalesi is a medieval structure on the shore.

column2: A Laz place name; the Turkish pronunciation of the Laz form Art'aşeni
column3: The town where the Fırtına River empties into the Black Sea is the Turkicized form of the Laz name Art'aşeni; Laz is a South Caucasian language related to Georgian and the source of many place names in the region. The Ottoman arched bridges of the Fırtına Valley and the Hemşin summer pastures lie within the district.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Laz place name Xopa; the harbor on the Georgian border
column3: Turkey's northeasternmost harbor is known by the Laz name Xopa; the Laz sound x became h in Turkish. Attached to Batumi in the Ottoman period, the town became a border town after 1878. It is known for the Sarp border gate and its tea factories.

column2: Georgian Şavşeti "land of the Shavsh": the name of a region of the Georgian Bagratid kingdom
column3: The mountainous region that appears as Şavşeti in the Georgian chronicles contains medieval Georgian churches and fortresses, among them the Tbeti Church. The Ottomans took the region in the 16th century, and the name became Şavşat in Turkish. Karagöl and the Sahara plateau are the district's natural heritage.

column2: From the name of the heir apparent Yusuf İzzeddin Efendi, "Yusuf's land"; Arabic Yūsuf + Turkish el "homeland"
column3: The Kiskim district in the Çoruh valley was given the name Yusufeli in 1914 after Yusuf İzzeddin Efendi, the heir apparent of the day; the element -eli, as in Kocaeli and Tunceli, is the Turkish word el meaning "homeland". Georgian churches (İşhan, Barhal) and the Çoruh, a rafting river, are the district's heritage; the old town was submerged beneath a dam reservoir in 2023.

column2: Armenian gayl "wolf" + get "river": "wolf river"; Greek Lykos is a translation of the same meaning
column3: The Kelkit River, the longest tributary of the Yeşilırmak, bore in antiquity the Greek name Lykos, "wolf"; Armenian Gayl-get carries the same meaning, and Turkish Kelkit derives from this form. The town in the river's source valley was a pass open to Turkish raids from before 1071; the legionary camp of Satala in the village of Sadak belongs to the Roman period.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of Greek Ionopolis "city of Ionia"; the earlier name was Abonouteichos
column3: Abonouteichos, the setting of Lucian's tale of the false prophet Alexander, took the name Ionopolis in the 2nd century at the prophet's request; Turkish İnebolu preserves the -polis element of this name as bolu. It received the Medal of Independence as the harbor where weapons from Istanbul were landed in Anatolia during the War of Independence; Atatürk began his Hat Reform journey from here.

column2: Turkish taş "stone" + köprü "bridge": from the stone bridge over the Gökırmak; the ancient name was Pompeiopolis
column3: The ruins of Pompeiopolis, founded in Paphlagonia by the Roman general Pompey in 64 BC, lie at Zımbıllı Tepe; the Turkish town took its name from the Seljuk-era stone bridge over the Gökırmak. It is known throughout Turkey for its garlic production; the word köprü comes from the Old Turkic form köprüg.

column2: Greek Herakleia "city of Herakles": the city of the Acheron cave, where Herakles was believed to have dragged Cerberus up from the underworld
column3: Heraclea Pontica, founded by the Megarians in 560 BC, stands beside the Acheron cave (Cehennemağzı, "mouth of hell") from which, according to legend, Herakles brought up the underworld hound Cerberus. The city, which the Genoese called Pontaraclia, passed to the Ottomans in 1360; the Turkish name Ereğli is distinguished from the Ereğlis of Konya and Marmara by the word Karadeniz. The discovery of coal in 1829 and the iron and steel works form the city's modern identity.

column2: From the name of the Thermodon River in the legendary land of the Amazons
column3: Greek legend places Themiskyra, capital of the Amazons, at the mouth of the Thermodon River; Herodotus and Strabo describe this river. The name, Terme in Turkish, was given to both the town and the river. The town east of the Çarşamba Plain is known for rice farming.

column2: From the name of Zela, the Pontic city famed for its temple of Anaitis; the site of the battle after which Caesar said "veni, vidi, vici"
column3: Zela, temple city of the Persian goddess Anaitis, was the site of the battle in 47 BC in which Julius Caesar defeated King Pharnaces of Pontus and wrote to Rome "I came, I saw, I conquered". The town, Zile in Turkish, became famous in Ottoman times for its grape molasses; its fortress and Roman theater stand on the mound.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of Greek Neokaisareia "city of the new Caesar"
column3: Kabeira, where the palace of King Mithridates of Pontus stood, took the name Neokaisareia in the Roman period; in the 4th century it was the episcopal city of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus. Danişmend Gazi made the city his capital in the 11th century; the name became Niksar, and the fortress of Niksar is described in the Danişmendnâme. It is known for its Ayvaz spring water and walnut production.

column2: Turkish boy "clan, tribe" + Persian ābād "prosperous place": a place where a Turkmen clan settled
column3: The name of the town in the Gökırmak valley combines Turkish boy "clan" with the Persian element -abad "prosperous", recalling the Turkmen clans that settled in the area in the Seljuk period. Its fortress dates from the Paphlagonian period; the Boyabat rock tombs and rice cultivation are the town's emblems.

column2: From the name of Akça Koca, the commander who led the earliest Ottoman conquests; Turkish akça "white" + koca "elder, great"
column3: The Byzantine town of Diapolis was known in the Ottoman period as Akçaşehir; in 1934 it was given the name of Akça Koca, who conquered Kocaeli in the reign of Orhan Gazi and whose tomb is here. Hazelnut orchards and the Genoese Castle are the town's emblems; the Turkish word koca derives from Old Turkic koca "old, venerable".

column2: Arabic vakf-ı kebîr "great endowment": because the town's land belonged to a large religious endowment
column3: The town on Büyükliman Bay west of Trabzon was known in the Ottoman period by the Arabic name Vakf-ı Kebir, "great endowment", because its land was property whose revenues were assigned to a large waqf. Vakfıkebir bread and butter are synonymous with the town; in antiquity another harbor named Kerasous is reported to have existed in the area.

column2: Origin disputed; associated with the ancient settlement of Paura or with a Greek place name
column3: The town on the Kızılırmak delta appears in Ottoman documents under the name Bafra; the name has been traced to the ancient settlement of Paura or to a Greek word, but the evidence is inconclusive. The İkiztepe mound dates back to the Bronze Age; tobacco and pide flatbread are the town's emblems. The Kızılırmak Delta bird sanctuary is on the UNESCO tentative list.

column2: Origin disputed; associated with Armenian Marzvan or with Persian merz "border" in the sense of "borderland"
column3: The plains town west of Amasya is written Marzvan in Armenian sources and Merzifon in Ottoman documents; whether the name is connected to Persian merz "border" or goes back to an older Anatolian name is debated. The complex of Kara Mustafa Paşa and the madrasa of Murad II are Ottoman works; Anatolia College was founded here in the 19th century.

column2: Armenian Ani, the name of a fortress and city associated with the Iranian goddess Anahit
column3: Ani, on the edge of the Arpaçay valley, became the capital of the Bagratid Armenian Kingdom in 961 and was known as "the city of a thousand and one churches"; its name derives from an old fortress name linked to the cult of Anahit. The Seljuks took the city in 1064, and the first Turkish mosque in Anatolia, the Menuçehr Mosque, was built here. The Mongol invasion and earthquakes left the city deserted; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

column2: Turkish sarı "yellow" + kamış "reed": a place of yellow reed beds; the site of the Sarıkamış Campaign of 1914
column3: The name of the town at the foot of the Allahuekber Mountains comes from the yellow reed beds in its meadows and marshes. Under Russian rule from 1878 to 1918 it grew around the barracks of Tsarist officers; in December 1914 the campaign in which the Ottoman army suffered enormous losses to freezing took place in these mountains. Scots pine forests and a ski resort form its present-day identity.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the fortress name Oltisi in Georgian sources; the home of Oltu stone (black amber)
column3: The fortress of Oltisi, in the Georgian region of Tao-Klarjeti in the Çoruh basin, appears in medieval chronicles; in Turkish it became Oltu. It remained under Russian rule from 1878 to 1918. The black amber quarried in the area, "Oltu stone", is used for prayer beads and jewelry; the fortress stands above the town.

column2: From the Armenian regional name Sper; the Syspiritis that Strabo mentions for its gold mines
column3: İspir, in the upper Çoruh valley, corresponds to the region of Syspiritis, famed in Strabo for its gold mines; the Armenian name Sper is linked to the origins of the Bagratid dynasty. Its fortress was repaired in the Seljuk and Saltukid periods, and the name became İspir in Turkish. It is known for its summer pastures and Çoruh rafting courses.

column2: From the name of the Armenian plain of Basean; the Ottoman name Hasankale derives from the fortress of the Akkoyunlu ruler Hasan
column3: The source plain of the Aras appears in Armenian sources as Basean and became Pasin in Turkish. In the Ottoman period the town bore the name Hasankale after the fortress repaired by the Akkoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan in the 15th century; it became Pasinler in the 1930s. The Battle of Pasinler in 1048 was the first major Seljuk victory over Byzantium; the town's hot springs are famous.

column2: From the name of Tušpa, capital of the Kingdom of Urartu; given in 2013 to the newly created central district
column3: Tušpa, founded on the rock of Van Castle in the 9th century BC, was the capital of the Urartian kings; its rock tombs and cuneiform inscriptions are on the citadel. The name, which survived in the Armenian form Tosp, was given in 2013 as Tuşba to one of Van's central districts. Lake Van is called "the sea of Tušpa" in Urartian texts.

column2: From the Armenian island name Aghtamar; legend ties it to the cry "Ah Tamar!" of a youth swimming to his beloved
column3: On the small island in Lake Van, the Church of the Holy Cross, built in 915–921 by King Gagik of Vaspurakan, is a masterpiece of Armenian art for the reliefs on its outer walls. The name is explained by the legend of a youth who swam every night to a girl named Tamar living on the island and cried "Ah Tamar!" as he drowned; this is a folk etymology. The church was restored in 2007 and became a museum.

column2: From the Armenian city name Arčēš; associated with Arṣaškun of the Urartian period
column3: The city on the northern shore of Lake Van appears as Arčēš in Armenian sources and Arjīsh in Arabic ones; it is associated with Arṣaškun, the capital of the Urartian king Arame. When the lake's waters rose the old city was submerged, and the town was moved north in the 19th century. The Karakoyunlu ruler Kara Yusuf was born here; the Çelebibağı cemetery is a medieval monument.

column2: Turkish göl "lake" + the name of the city of Van; Urartian "sea of Tušpa", Greek Thospitis
column3: Turkey's largest lake is referred to in Urartian texts by the name of the capital Tušpa; Strabo and Ptolemy write Thospitis. Because of its soda-rich water the lake was called "Van Deryası" (the Sea of Van) in Ottoman documents, as if it were a sea; it holds Akdamar Island and the pearl mullet. The word göl appears in the Orkhon Inscriptions in the Old Turkic form köl.

column2: Turkey's highest mountain (5,137 m); the biblical name Ararat derives from the name of the Kingdom of Urartu, and the Armenian name is Masis
column3: The name of the kingdom that appears in Assyrian annals as Urarṭu lived on in the Bible as the mountains of Ararat, where Noah's ark came to rest; the Armenians called the mountain Masis and the Turks Ağrı Dağı. Marco Polo speaks of the mountain's never-melting snow, and Evliya Çelebi describes its appearance from Van. The connection of the Turkish word ağrı to the mountain is explained through the sense "great, lofty"; the first ascent was made by Parrot in 1829.

column2: From the name of Bayezid, son of the Jalayirid Sultan Ahmed (or of Yıldırım Bayezid); the word Doğu "East" was added in 1934
column3: The town on the site of the Urartian fortress of Daroynk took the name Bayezid at the end of the 14th century, when Bayezid of the Jalayirid dynasty repaired the fortress; it appears in Ottoman documents as the sanjak of Bâyezîd. The palace of Çıldıroğlu İshak Paşa, completed in 1784, is one of the last great monuments of Ottoman architecture. In 1934 the name was changed to Doğubayazıt to avoid confusion with Yenişehir Bayezid in Bursa. The name Bayezid comes from Arabic Bāyazīd.

column2: Armenian Manazkert "fortress of Manaz": a name linked to the fortress founded by the Urartian king Menua
column3: The plains town north of the Murat River appears in Armenian sources as Manazkert and is associated with the name of the Urartian king Menua; the element -kert means "founder, maker" in Armenian. The Battle of Malazgirt (Manzikert) on 26 August 1071, in which Sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos Diogenes, is regarded as the beginning of the Turkification of Anatolia. Its fortress and Great Mosque still stand in the town.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Armenian city name Khlat, via Arabic Khilāṭ; the city famed for its Seljuk tombstones
column3: Ahlat on the western shore of Lake Van was known as Khlat in Armenian and Khilāṭ in Arabic; in the 12th and 13th centuries it was the capital of the Ahlatshahs and was praised as "Kubbetü'l-İslam" (the Dome of Islam). The tombstones and domed mausoleums of its Seljuk cemetery, famed for their stonework, are on the UNESCO tentative list. In 1071 Alp Arslan marched from here with his army to Malazgirt.

column2: Origin disputed; a Turkicized form either of the Armenian village name Datvan or of a construction "land of the Tats" with Turkish tat "foreigner"
column3: The town at the southwestern tip of Lake Van appears in Ottoman documents in the form Tatvan; the name is traced either to an Armenian village name or to the word tat, used in Old Turkic for non-Turkish settled peoples. The Nemrut crater lake and the ferry port operating since 1971 form the town's identity; the Van Gölü Express crosses to Van by ferry from here.

column2: Turkish yüksek "high" + ova "plain": from the plain at 1,900 meters; the earlier name was Kurdish Gever
column3: The town on the high plain between the Cilo and Sat mountains was known by the Kurdish name Gever; in 1936 it was given the name Yüksekova, describing the plain's altitude. The word yüksek is Old Turkic yüksek, while ova is related to the word oba. The plain, home to Nestorian and Kurdish tribes, is one of the coldest places in Turkey.

column2: Armenian khar "rock" + berd "fortress": "rock fortress"; associated with Ḫarputa in Urartian inscriptions
column3: The old city on the rocky hill above Elazığ bears the Armenian name Kharberd, meaning "rock fortress"; Arab sources called it Ḥiṣn Ziyād, "fortress of Ziyad". The Artuqid Great Mosque (1156) and the Süt Kalesi (Milk Castle) are the city's monuments. When the administration moved down to the plain in 1862, Harput emptied out; Harput music and the "Çayda Çıra" dance keep its culture alive.

column2: Turkish arslan "lion" + tepe "hill": from the Late Hittite lion statues found on the mound; the ancient name was Melid
column3: The mound beside Malatya housed one of the world's oldest palace structures in the 4th millennium BC; the gate lions of the Late Hittite kingdom of Melid gave the mound its Turkish name. The word arslan appears in the Orkhon Inscriptions in the Old Turkic form arslan and passed into Hungarian as oroszlán. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2021.

column2: From the city name Taranta in Hittite texts; the fortress town in the valley of the Tohma River
column3: The fortress town in the valley carved by the Tohma River is identified with Taranta of the Hittite documents; Byzantine and Arab sources carried the same name forward. The Zengibar Castle and the complex of Somuncu Baba (Şeyh Hamid-i Veli) form the town's memory; the Gürpınar Waterfall is the valley's natural beauty.

column2: From the Armenian fortress name Kamakh; Ani-Kamakh, the sacred city of the temple of Anaitis
column3: The rock fortress in a narrow gorge of the Euphrates is known in Armenian sources as Ani-Kamakh and was famed for its temple of the Persian goddess Anaitis and the tombs of the Arsacid kings. The tomb of Mengücek Gazi dates from the Seljuk period; the town appears in Ottoman documents as the sanjak of Kemah. Kemah tulum cheese is associated with the town.

column2: The Turkish pronunciation of the Armenian place name Kaghzvan; the salt-mining town in the Aras valley
column3: The town south of the Aras River appears in Armenian sources as Kaghzvan and became Kağızman in Turkish. Salt mines dating from the Byzantine and Seljuk periods have been worked for centuries. The rock paintings at Camuşlu are the region's prehistoric witness; the Kağızman apple is a local product.

column2: From the regional name Çıldır, of Georgian origin; the highland lake at the center of the Ottoman province of Çıldır
column3: Turkey's highest large lake lies in the region that gave its name to the Ottoman province of Çıldır, centered on Ahıska (Akhaltsikhe); the regional name derives from a Georgian place name. In the Battle of Çıldır in 1578 Lala Mustafa Paşa defeated the Safavids. In winter horse-drawn sleds run and ice fishing is practiced on the frozen lake; the island of Akçakale carries a medieval fortress.

column2: Turkish palan "packsaddle, saddle pad" (Persian pālān) + döken "that sheds": the mountain so steep it throws off the packsaddles of pack animals
column3: The name of the 3,271-meter mountain south of Erzurum is attributed to the steepness of its passes, which caused pack animals to shed their saddles (palan); the word palan comes from Persian pālān. Evliya Çelebi describes the mountain's cold. A ski resort since the 1990s, the mountain hosted the Winter Universiade in 2011.

column2: From Sumerian Buranun / Akkadian Purattu "great river"; Turkish Fırat via Arabic al-Furāt
column3: The river that was the lifeblood of the Mesopotamian civilizations appears in Sumerian tablets as Buranun and in Akkadian texts as Purattu; Greek Euphrates derives from this name. The Arabs called it al-Furāt, and Turkish Fırat comes from this form. Formed by the junction of the Karasu and Murat branches at Keban, the river is counted among the rivers of paradise in the Quran and the Bible; the Keban and Atatürk dams stand on it.

column2: From Sumerian Idigna "swift-flowing river"; Turkish Dicle via Arabic Dijla, Greek Tigris "tiger, arrow"
column3: The name of the river called Idigna in Sumerian and Idiglat in Akkadian was reinterpreted in Old Persian through the word Tigrā "arrow" and passed into Greek as Tigris; the Arabic form Dijla became Dicle in Turkish. The river, flowing past the foot of the walls of Diyarbakır, passes Hasankeyf and descends into Iraq; the On Gözlü (Ten-Arched) Bridge (1065) is a Marwanid work. The Ilısu Dam reservoir filled in 2019.

column2: From the name of Munzur Baba, held sacred in local belief; origin disputed
column3: The mountain range covering the north of Tunceli is associated with the legend of Munzur Baba, held sacred in Alevi belief; the miracles of the shepherd Munzur live on in the dialects of Dersim. Whether the name comes from Zazaki or from an older language is debated. Munzur Valley National Park is famous for the springs at the source of the Munzur River.

column2: From Matiate "city of caves" in the Assyrian annals; Syriac Midyad
column3: Midyat, center of the Tur Abdin plateau, appears in the annals of the Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II as Matiate; the name is explained as "caves", which fits the city's rock-cut cellars. Syriac Orthodox churches (the Mor Gabriel Monastery, since 397) and stone mansions are the city's identity, and its telkâri filigree silverwork is famous. Syriac, Arabic, Kurdish and Turkish are spoken side by side.

column2: From the city name Naṣibina in the Assyrian annals; the city of the Syriac School of Nisibis
column3: The city that appears as Naṣibina in Assyrian sources was besieged repeatedly on the Roman-Persian frontier; Nisibis, ceded by Rome to the Persians in 363, housed the famous theological school of the Church of the East. The Mor Yakup Church (4th century) and the Zeynel Abidin Mosque are the city's monuments; the Arabic form Naṣībīn became Nusaybin in Turkish. Across the border lies the Syrian city of Qamishli.

column2: Arabic ḥiṣn "fortress" + Syriac kepha "rock": "rock fortress"
column3: The city in the rocky valley of the Tigris was known by the Syriac name Kepha, "rock"; the Arabs called it Ḥiṣn Kayfā, "rock fortress", and in Turkish folk pronunciation Hasankeyf was assimilated to the personal name Hasan. The Artuqid bridge, the Ayyubid mosques and the Zeynel Bey Tomb were the city's monuments; in 2020 the waters of the Ilısu Dam covered the old city, and the monuments were moved to the new settlement.

column2: Akkadian ḫarrānu "road, caravan route": the city at the crossroads of the caravan routes
column3: Harran, one of the oldest cities of Mesopotamia, takes its name from the Akkadian word for "road"; it appears in the Bible as the city where Abraham stayed on his way to Canaan. The temple of the moon god Sin and the Harran madrasa, counted among the world's first universities, were founded here; the Roman general Crassus was defeated by the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 BC. The beehive houses are the city's emblem.

column2: Turkish göbek "navel, belly" + -li + tepe "hill": "hill with a navel", from the rounded mound at its center
column3: The hill northeast of Şanlıurfa holds the world's oldest temple structures, dated to 9600 BC; its T-shaped pillars were carved before the invention of writing and agriculture. Its Turkish name comes from the mound rising like a navel at the center of the hill; the Kurdish name Xirabreşk, "black ruin", is also used. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.

column2: From Aramaic birtha "fortress, citadel"; the fortress town on the Euphrates, with the Turkish diminutive suffix -cik
column3: The fortress town on the western bank of the Euphrates was known by the Aramaic name birtha, "fortress"; the Turkish suffix -cik was added to the Arabic form al-Bīra to give Birecik. The fortress on the Mamluk-Ottoman frontier fell to Selim I in 1516; its bridge over the Euphrates was built in 1956. The last nesting ground of the bald ibis (kelaynak) is here.

column2: Origin disputed; the Turkish pronunciation of a Syriac or Arabic place name, the town opposite Rumkale
column3: The town on the bank of the Euphrates lies opposite Rumkale (Arabic Kalʿat ar-Rūm), which the Armenian Catholicosate made its seat in the 12th and 13th centuries; the origin of the name Halfeti is not known for certain. In 2000 the Birecik Dam submerged the old town, and the "sunken city" is visited by boat tours. It is known for its black rose.

column2: From the Syriac regional name Sarug; the homeland of the Syriac poet Jacob (Mor Yakup of Sarug)
column3: The plain southwest of Urfa is known by the Syriac name Sarug and lives on in church literature through the name of the 6th-century Syriac poet-bishop Jacob of Serugh; it was called Batnai in the Roman period and Sarūj in the Arab period. A district of the sanjak of Urfa under the Ottomans, the town lies opposite Kobani on the Syrian border.

column2: Persian vīrān "ruined" + şahr "city": the "ruined city" on the ruins of ancient Constantina
column3: The city that the Syriacs called Tella bore the name Constantina in the Byzantine period and was destroyed in the Persian wars of the 6th century. Known in Ottoman times as "viran şehir" for its ruins, the site became a town again in the 19th century with the settlement of the Milli tribe; both elements of the name are Persian. The ruins of the octagonal Byzantine church stand in the middle of the town.

column2: Turkish ceylan "gazelle" (from Persian) + pınar "spring": from the gazelles living in the area; the earlier name was Arabic Raʾs al-ʿAyn "head of the spring"
column3: The ancient city at the source springs of the Habur River was known by the Syriac and Arabic names Rēš ʿAynā / Raʾs al-ʿAyn, meaning "head of the spring". When the border divided the town in the 1920s, the part remaining in Turkey was named Ceylanpınar, inspired by the local gazelle herds; the word ceylan comes from Persian cerān. The state farm here is Turkey's largest agricultural enterprise.

column2: Armenian sev "black" + averak "ruin": "black ruin"; from the town's basalt fortress
column3: The town at the foot of the Karacadağ volcano takes its Armenian name Sevaverak, "black ruin", from its fortress of basalt stone; Arabic Suwaydāʾ, "blackish", describes the same color. Attached to the province of Diyarbekir under the Ottomans, the town became Siverek in Turkish. Its fortress and the Çarşı Mosque are its historic buildings.

column2: The origin of the name Silvan is disputed; earlier names were Armenian Nprkert, Greek Martyropolis "city of martyrs" and Arabic Meyyafarikin
column3: The city east of Diyarbakır took the name Martyropolis, "city of martyrs", in the 5th century when Bishop Maruthas brought the bones of the Persian martyrs here; the Arabs called it Mayyāfāriqīn. It served as a capital under the Marwanids and the Artuqids; the Malabadi Bridge of Saladin's era is nearby. The origin of the Turkish name Silvan is not known for certain.
